displayQuote: If you think you understand quantum mechanics, you don't understand quantum mechanics

meta.title: Who really said "If you think you understand quantum mechanics, you don't understand quantum mechanics"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No source exists for this epigram. What Feynman actually wrote is quieter: 'I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics' (1965).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you think you understand quantum mechanics, you don't understand quantum mechanics'?
meta.ogDescription: Universally credited to Feynman, sourced to nothing. His documented line, in The Character of Physical Law (1965), says something gentler and better.

answer.label: Feynman’s idea — but not Feynman’s words
answer.sourceLine: This is a right-person, wrong-words case. Feynman really did say that quantum mechanics defeats understanding — but not in these words, and nobody who repeats them has ever produced a source. The sentence appears in none of the sourced sections of his Wikiquote entry, and editors there have been asking for a citation since 2011 without one surfacing. What he actually wrote is ‘I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics’, in The Character of Physical Law (1965), chapter 6, page 129 — the book of the Messenger Lectures he gave at Cornell in 1964.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: ‘I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics’
The Character of Physical Law (1965), ch. 6, ‘Probability and Uncertainty — the Quantum Mechanical View of Nature’, p. 129
Messenger Lectures, Cornell University, 1964; recorded by the BBC

source.excerpt: There might have been a time when only one man did, because he was the only guy who caught on, before he wrote his paper. But after people read the paper a lot of people understood the theory of relativity in some way or other, certainly more than twelve. On the other hand, I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.
trail: The genuine sentence has a clean citation: chapter 6 of The Character of Physical Law, ‘Probability and Uncertainty — the Quantum Mechanical View of Nature’, page 129, as recorded in the sourced section of Feynman’s Wikiquote entry the citation ↗.

The popular epigram has no such anchor. It is absent from every sourced section of that same entry, and the talk page carries a thread opened in February 2011 by an editor who found roughly 16,500 exact-phrase matches for it online, skimmed them, saw almost all crediting Feynman by name — and could not find one that actually gave a source the sourcing thread ↗.

The epigram is often assumed to descend from Niels Bohr, and that suggestion is made on the Feynman talk page itself, where an editor proposes it is a paraphrase of a line credited to Bohr the suggestion ↗. Bohr’s own saying — ‘anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it’ — is filed by Wikiquote under Disputed as well, resting on Werner Heisenberg’s recollection of a 1952 conversation in Physics and Beyond (1971), p. 206. It is a separate saying with its own attribution problem Bohr, disputed ↗.

We could not open the book itself to re-check page 129: the Internet Archive’s copy of the 1965 M.I.T. Press edition is lending-restricted, so the page number here rests on Wikiquote’s citation rather than on our own reading the edition record ↗.
source.excerptNote: The genuine passage, with the sentence in the position that gives it its force. He is contrasting quantum mechanics with relativity, which he says plenty of people understood once they had read the paper. The joke lands on the mock-cautious “I think I can safely say” — a man measuring exactly how large a claim he is about to make.

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Richard Feynman and MIT Press
source.rightsNote: The genuine sentence is in copyright. The Character of Physical Law was first published in 1965 and has been continuously in print, so it is protected in the United States, with rights administered through Feynman’s estate and his publishers. Short quotation with attribution is ordinary practice; reproducing the passage at length is not. The popular epigram has no identified author, so no term can be calculated for it — that is a gap in the record, not a licence. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Richard Feynman
author.heading: About Richard Feynman
author.bio: Richard Feynman (1918–1988) shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on quantum electrodynamics, and was probably the most quotable physicist of his century — a lecturer who talked about the hardest subject in science with cheerful irreverence. That reputation is exactly why this sentence sticks to him: it sounds like something he would say. He did say something like it. He just said it with more modesty and less paradox.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Nothing here was invented from nothing. A real remark by a real physicist was tightened into a paradox, and the paradox travelled better than the original.

items.why: It appears in none of the sourced sections of Feynman’s Wikiquote entry. A talk-page thread opened in February 2011 records an editor finding roughly 16,500 exact-phrase matches online, almost all naming Feynman — and reports being unable to find one that gave a source the thread ↗.

items.who: A documented sentence, one step away
items.why: ‘I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics’ — The Character of Physical Law (1965), ch. 6, p. 129. The popular version rewrites this as a self-referential trap, which is wittier and says something he did not say the citation ↗.

Feynman’s sentence includes him: nobody understands it, himself included, said a year before he shared a Nobel Prize for work in the field. The epigram turns that into a standard other people fail — if you feel you understand, you are disqualified. Same subject, different posture.

Bohr is credited with ‘anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it’, which Wikiquote also files as Disputed, resting on Heisenberg’s account of a 1952 conversation in Physics and Beyond (1971), p. 206. It is not the source of the Feynman epigram Bohr, disputed ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No one who quotes these words has produced a source for them. Feynman’s documented line is ‘I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics’ — The Character of Physical Law (1965), chapter 6, page 129 the citation ↗.

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: Quantum mechanics is the one part of physics whose predictions are impeccable and whose meaning is still argued over, so a licence to stop trying to picture it arrives as relief. That is most of the appeal.

The rewrite adds something the original refuses. Feynman was describing a limit on intuition, his own included. The epigram converts that into an entrance exam with no pass mark — anyone who feels they understand is thereby wrong. It is a better joke and a worse thought.
detailsBody: 1964: Feynman gives the Messenger Lectures at Cornell; the BBC records them.
1965: they are published as The Character of Physical Law. Chapter 6, page 129 — ‘I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.’
1971: Heisenberg’s Physics and Beyond reports Bohr, in 1952, on not being shocked by quantum theory — the other saying this one gets confused with.
February 2011: a Wikiquote editor documents the epigram in wide circulation, crediting Feynman, with no source anyone can supply.
context.pull: He said nobody understands it, and counted himself in. The rewrite makes it a test you fail by passing.
